_: CURATED JUDGEMENT ONLY. Every other field on the page is read out of the code by gen_deep_research_schema.py. Ratings are opinions and have to be argued for; keeping them here means a reader can always tell which is which. Ratings reflect the state on 2026-09-09, after the verification build and before run 7.

runner.how: The live path. Picks up turns that are due, asks chat, extracts fields, judges them, opens the cited documents, asks the registry whether those documents govern the line, reads the drafter's own reasoning, and decides whether to go round again.
findings: good
The only entry point carrying all five guarantees. Everything built on 2026-09-08 lands here.
bad
It is ONE of five ways to run a turn. A request answered through run_v2 is judged without any document ever being opened, and nothing warns anybody.
bad
The document-side gate existed, was tested, and was never called from this file until 2026-09-08 — the docstring of critique() had promised it ran for months.
good
Now writes the stance when a request settles, at both settle points — which is what makes `stance` on a status poll a fact rather than a field name.

extract_critique.how: Pulls typed fields out of chat's prose, then checks each one: is the quote really in the answer, was the document really cited, is the source authoritative enough for this caller, and does the quote actually support this value.
findings: good
Gates are ordered and each one names what it answers, so a refusal says which question failed.
good
An absence is now evidenced by having READ the governing rule rather than by quoting one, which is the only way a true negative can ever pass.
bad
`scope` was extracted and then dropped from the verdict record, so three scoped facts read as one field with three values and the corpus looked self-contradictory.
bad
`_schema_gap` is requested in the prompt and appeared exactly once in the whole repository — in the prompt asking for it. The model complied and nothing read it.

corroborate.how: Opens the document a claim cites and decides whether it really says it, by reading the passages most likely to carry it.
findings: bad

Returned `absent` — the document does not say it — when passage SELECTION found nothing to read. Seven of eleven document-gate refusals in one run were that, including a claim the rule states verbatim.
good
Now returns `undecidable` with read=0, and `absent` requires that passages were read and refused.

locate.how: Finds the line in a document that a claim rests on and cites it by page, paragraph and character offset, instead of handing back a scored excerpt.
findings: good
Numbers, codes and short acronyms are tokens at last: 21, 365/6, H2017 and APR-DRG were invisible to the old pattern, which is what refused an eligibility rule the document states.
good
Never snaps a citation on score alone. The top-scoring span for one real claim was the wrong sentence; a reader picks and the snap follows the reader.
unproven
Written 2026-09-09 and not yet exercised in a completed run. Its outcome vocabulary is argued for, not measured.

recommend.how: Says what a reader should DO with a result — usable, verify first, the evidence conflicts, the rule offers a choice, nobody checked — from signals the other actors already recorded. Costs nothing; the work was done and never summarised.
findings: good
No model call. Every signal is already in the record.
good
Tells a LIST from a CONFLICT, and a rule that offers branches from a corpus contradicting itself — three checks in this module had confused those.
bad
Had NO CALLER for a day — written, rated green, and never run. The defect this module exists to name, inside the module that names it. The runner now calls it when a request settles.
bad

Run at last over the 58 requests holding a verdict: not one came back usable. 32 requests say status='sourced'; 24 of those are `unverified` (nothing ever opened the cited document) and 8 `inconclusive`. All predate the document gate, so the reading is honest — but 'sourced' has been read as 'answered' for three weeks.

read_thinking.how: Reads the drafter's own reasoning for shapes that recur — it conceded then asserted anyway, it named two populations, it named a rule it never cited, it ran the same search four times — and turns each into the next question.
findings: good
Quotes the drafter back to itself, which is harder to wave away than an instruction to try harder.
good
Every reader of the reasoning trace before this was a RENDERER. No actor consumed it.

thinking.how: Lets every actor record what it saw, what it made of that, and what it decided — kept as three separate fields so a wrong decision can be traced to bad input or bad reasoning.
findings: good
The judge now records as much reasoning per question as the drafter does.
unproven
Three actors write traces. Nine of the twelve named actors still record nothing.

diagnose.how: Works out WHY a question failed — is the rule missing, is it held but unreadable, did we answer about the wrong service, is our own schema the blocker — and says what would fix it.
findings: good
Every branch returns through one place, so a gate added later cannot forget to record its reasoning.
bad
authority_tier called the RIGHT rule the wrong one whenever a request carried no rule reference — nothing was compared, and all five fields of one question were refused on it.
unproven
Instrumented on 2026-09-09 and has not fired once in six runs.

resolution.how: Holds what happens after a verdict — the options a caller can choose between, the ruling they made, and whether that closes the question or reopens it.
findings: good
A decision is a contract a service can call, not only a button a person can press.
bad
A promise generated from a TERMINAL set rather than written down once let 'stop asking' reopen the question.

run_v2.how: An older way to run a turn. Still judges answers, and never opens a document, asks the registry, or records reasoning.
findings: bad
1 of 5 guarantees. An answer produced here is judged against the ANSWER only — no document is ever opened — and nothing on the result says so.
bad
Five entry points run a turn and only one is complete. This is where a gate with no caller hides.

run_batch.how: Runs a set of questions together. Opens documents, but records no reasoning and never asks the registry.
findings: bad
2 of 5 guarantees. It called the document gate for months while the live runner did not, which is exactly why nobody noticed the live path had none.

console.how: The page a person reads: every question, every round, what each actor did, what it cost and what is waiting on somebody.
findings: good
Generated from one source, with assertions, after two variants of the same page drifted apart.
bad
Ten uses of design tokens that do not exist rendered transparent, and a sticky header let rows show through it.

language.how: One place that decides what every state, actor and refusal is CALLED, so the machine's vocabulary and the reader's are the same words.
findings: good
The reader is a front-end user, not an engineer, and the names are chosen for them.

recorder.how: Writes the ledger — who did what, in which round, with the evidence attached.
findings: good
Every event carries an actor name, so the trace reads as a sequence of decisions rather than a log.

contract.how: Declares the four verbs a caller can use — submit, check status, decide, close out — and the five surfaces that render them, once, in one file. Published to a table so the router validates against it instead of restating it.
findings: good
Seven code paths could create a request and one of them checked anything. This is the declaration the eighth — the HTTP door — reads at request time, so it cannot drift from what the page shows.
good
The UX is declared beside the verbs it calls, so a surface rendering an API that does not exist fails the build rather than a demo.
unproven
Written 2026-09-09. Six ungated insert paths still exist; the invariant names them rather than removing them.
good

A package since the framework landed — fields, verbs, surfaces, actions, specifics, notes, words, artifacts, authority, tools, decisions, tasks. The split failed the generator's own invariant on the first build, which is the check doing its job.

worklist.how: Turns what we advise on each question into the work somebody actually does — grouping many questions into one errand where they need the same document, and saying which rung of the ladder told us what that document is.
findings: good
39 questions carrying advice collapse into 8 activities, and the top one is worth 23 — an item invisible while it was 23 rows, because it looked like 23 problems.
good

A document class carries its own SCOPE. The corpus settles it: a provider manual is one row per payer, a 59G rule is one per service, a fee schedule is one per category. Four handbook errands were four requests for one document.
good

When nothing identifies a document, the activity is `explore` — research, not retrieval, and the only fetch-adjacent work that happens HERE rather than outside. 'Name the document' would have put the burden on somebody who already knows, and mostly nobody does.
bad

Derived from recommendations only, so it can hold only work the machine already knows how to advise. 'Call this person' cannot be derived — nothing in the record knows a person exists to call — and there is no route to declare one.
unproven
Priority is questions-unblocked plus overdue. Crude on purpose, and nobody has worked a single item, so the ordering has never been tested against what a person would actually pick up.

ux_data.how: Composes every request the UX shows — its artifacts, its actions, its notes — and the worklist derived from them, so the page has one source rather than a query per section.
findings: bad

Existed only as a script in a scratch directory. The page it feeds could be rebuilt by nobody but the session that wrote it — a generated artefact that cannot be regenerated, which is the failure this whole schematic exists to prevent, one layer out.
good
Lives in the skill rather than beside the generator: it reads research.* and composes contract + worklist. The skill owns what the data MEANS; the generator owns how it LOOKS.
good
Moving it changed the emitted page by zero bytes, which is the only evidence a refactor is a refactor.

journey.how: Answers the one question the status column answers worst: where is my request. Round by round — when each started, what it produced, how long it took, and which one stopped.
findings: bad
Measured when it was written: 16 turns in flight, 10 started more than six hours ago and never came back, four `waiting` for 69 hours. The request-level status on every one of them reads `open`.
bad

20 turns say `complete` and carry no settled timestamp, so any duration computed from them is the age of the universe rather than the length of the round. The page says the clock was lost rather than showing the number.
good
Reads only. A page that quietly restarted a stalled round while somebody was looking at it would be a page nobody could trust to describe the machine.
